It calculates aerodynamic drag as a function of car type or shape, rolling resistance as a function of weight, and curvature resistance or the resistance of wheels on a single axle slipping as they travel different distances traveling around a curve. The custom LTD algorithm used in SCORE is designed with a balance of computational efficiency and accuracy. The most significant change we made to traditional LTD calculations is replacing the integrating over time with distance. There are additional steps taken to improve computational efficiency. Many of properties that describe the route and consist are evaluated before integration. These properties do not change as a result of the states calculated during the integrations. The process used is as follows: 1. The drag coefficients for all car elements in the consist are combined to calculate drag as a function of speed. 2. The track resistance for the consist is calculated as a function of consist position (first car – locomotive) along the route. The drag coefficients are summed from the ordered list of cars in the consist. Each car type has a different drag coefficient. The track resistance is a function of rolling resistance, curvature and gradient over a specified location and length of the route. The next step in the analysis is to determine target speeds throughout the route. This is a two-step process. On first pass, the target speed for each segment is set to either the maximum speed permitted by the track conditions or a maximum speed set by the powering policy. A second pass is then used to potentially reduce target speed due to limitations in braking. The target speed needs to be reduced in segments prior to reductions in the maximum allowable speed. The target speed also needs to consider segments where the gradient is providing more power than the brakes can manage to maintain maximum speed. In general, it is assumed that dynamic and regenerative braking is maximized. Specifically, when determining target speeds, we assume 95% of maximum braking capabilities. The prior segment target speed is determined by first calculating the external forces for the current interval. These include the track drag as a function of position, the aerodynamic drag as a function speed (taken as the final target speed) and the forces from the track gradient. The maximum allowable braking force is then added to these forces. From this sum of forces and the total mass of the consist, the acceleration (in most cases a deceleration) is calculated for the interval. The target speed for the interval can then be set given the target speed for the next interval and the acceleration. This iterative process will keep moving back the route until the target speed for the interval is greater than or equal the maximum allowable speed set in the first pass.
